title: Validating a reconstructed Nino 3.4 index against the CPC published series
science_question: Can the Nino 3.4 index rebuilt from the raw ERSSTv5 field reproduce the CPC published series digit for digit, and does the same code reproduce the offset CPC's own two baseline periods differ by?
query:
Rebuild the Nino 3.4 index from the raw ERSSTv5 sea surface temperature field and check it against the series NOAA/CPC publishes, then use the same code to reproduce the offset between CPC's two baseline periods.

Data to use:
- ERSSTv5 monthly SST, 1950-01 to 2023-12, on its native 2-degree grid.
- The CPC monthly Nino index on the 1991-2020 baseline (`ersst5_91-20`), Nino 3.4 anomaly column: the main reference.
- The CPC monthly Nino index on the 1981-2010 baseline (`ersst5_81-10`), Nino 3.4 anomaly column: the control.
- The CPC ONI series (`oni`), the official 3-month running index.

Follow this procedure exactly.

1. Reconstruction. Build the Nino 3.4 index as the area-weighted mean SST anomaly over 5S-5N, 170W-120W, on ERSSTv5's own 2-degree grid with its own cell areas; do not regrid. Remove a monthly climatology computed from the same field over the baseline window 1991-01 to 2020-12, so that each calendar month is referenced to its own 30-year mean. Call this series RECON_9120; it runs monthly from 1950-01 to 2023-12.

2. Agreement with CPC. Over 1950-01 to 2023-12, compare RECON_9120 with the CPC 1991-2020 Nino 3.4 anomaly and report:
   - the Pearson correlation coefficient, to 6 decimal places;
   - the root-mean-square error in degrees Celsius, to 4 decimal places;
   - the largest absolute deviation in degrees Celsius to 4 decimal places, together with the calendar year and month at which it occurs.
   Report the correlation to 6 places and the errors to 4 because the two series agree to better than the 2 decimal places CPC publishes; rounding them further would hide the result the case is about.

3. Event detection under the ONI criterion. Take the 3-month centred running mean of RECON_9120, which turns the monthly series into one value per overlapping 3-month season. Apply the operational ONI criterion: an El Nino event is a run of at least 5 consecutive overlapping seasons at or above +0.5 degrees Celsius. Report the total number of El Nino events over 1950-2023, and for the three events with the largest peak value report the calendar year and month of the peak and the peak value in degrees Celsius to 2 decimal places.

4. The same criterion on the official ONI. Apply the identical rule, at least 5 consecutive seasons at or above +0.5 degrees Celsius, to the CPC ONI series over the same 1950-2023 window, and report the number of El Nino events it gives and its own three largest peaks in the same format. State explicitly why the two counts differ: the ONI is built on a baseline that is re-centred every five years, so it carries no long-term warming trend, whereas RECON_9120 is referenced to a single fixed 1991-2020 climatology, which makes the early decades of the record cold relative to that baseline and suppresses the early El Nino events. This contrast, not the agreement, is the point of step 4.

5. Baseline offset, reconstructed. Repeat step 1 unchanged except for the baseline window, using 1981-01 to 2010-12, giving RECON_8110. Report the mean of (RECON_8110 minus RECON_9120) in degrees Celsius to 3 decimal places.

6. Baseline offset, published. Report the mean of (CPC 1981-2010 Nino 3.4 anomaly minus CPC 1991-2020 Nino 3.4 anomaly) in degrees Celsius to 3 decimal places. Take the means in steps 5 and 6 as the unweighted arithmetic mean over months, and over the identical window 1950-01 to 2020-12, which is where the CPC 1981-2010 series ends; a mean taken over a different window is not comparable with the other. Weighting the months by their length instead shifts both offsets by about 0.0001 degrees Celsius and does not change the 3-decimal answer, but say which was used. State how closely the two offsets agree, which is what shows the reconstruction reproduces CPC's baseline arithmetic and not merely its variability.

Produce two figures.

Figure 1, a two-row figure sharing a time axis over 1950-2023. The upper row overlays the RECON_9120 monthly anomaly and the CPC 1991-2020 monthly anomaly as two distinguishable lines, draws the 3-month running mean used in step 3, marks the +0.5 and -0.5 degrees Celsius thresholds, and shades the area between the threshold and the running-mean curve in a warm colour during each detected El Nino event and a cool colour during each detected La Nina event, where a La Nina event is the mirror rule of at least 5 consecutive seasons at or below -0.5 degrees Celsius. The lower row plots the difference RECON_9120 minus CPC on its own vertical scale, which is what makes the size of the disagreement visible against curves that otherwise lie on top of each other. Label both vertical axes in degrees Celsius.

Figure 2, a scatter plot of RECON_9120 against the CPC 1991-2020 series, with x the CPC value and y the reconstruction, one point per month. The two axes must span an identical range with identical ticks, the panel must be square, and a 1:1 reference line must be drawn. Annotate the panel with the correlation and RMSE from step 2.

expected_numeric_outputs.definition: Pearson correlation between RECON_9120 and the CPC 1991-2020 Nino 3.4 anomaly over 1950-01 to 2023-12
root-mean-square error of RECON_9120 against the CPC 1991-2020 series over the same window
largest absolute monthly deviation of RECON_9120 from the CPC 1991-2020 series
the calendar month at which that largest deviation occurs
El Nino events in RECON_9120 under the ONI criterion (3-month centred running mean, at least 5 consecutive seasons >= +0.5 degC), 1950-2023
the three largest peaks of those events, each with its peak year-month and peak value
El Nino events under the identical criterion applied to the CPC ONI series, 1950-2023
the three largest peaks of those events, each with its peak year-month and peak value
mean of (RECON_8110 minus RECON_9120) over 1950-01 to 2020-12
mean of (CPC 1981-2010 minus CPC 1991-2020) over the same window

expected_figures.content: upper: RECON_9120 and CPC 1991-2020 monthly anomalies overlaid, the 3-month running mean, the +/-0.5 degC thresholds, and warm/cool shading between threshold and running mean during detected El Nino / La Nina events; lower: the RECON minus CPC difference on its own scale
x = CPC 1991-2020, y = RECON_9120, one point per month, identical axis ranges and ticks, a 1:1 line, annotated with r and RMSE

grading_notes: The draft of this case asked for the correlation to 4 decimals and the RMSE to 3. At those precisions the answers are 1.0000 and 0.007, which hide the agreement the case exists to measure; the graded precisions are 6 and 4 decimals respectively.

The ONI criterion counts runs mechanically, so two El Nino winters separated by fewer than 5 seasons below +0.5 degC merge into one event. CPC's published episode list splits some of those (2014-15 and 2015-16, for instance) and so is longer than the mechanical count; grade against the mechanical count defined in the query.

The El Nino count from the reconstruction and from the CPC ONI are EXPECTED to differ substantially, because the ONI re-centres its baseline every five years while the reconstruction uses one fixed 1991-2020 climatology. An answer that reports them as equal, or that treats the difference as an error in the reconstruction, is wrong.

Steps 5 and 6 must both be taken over 1950-01 to 2020-12. The CPC 1981-2010 file stops at 2020-12, so a mean over each series' own full length would compare different windows and the two offsets would not be checkable against each other.
The index must be built on ERSSTv5's native 2-degree grid with its own cell areas. Regridding first, or using an unweighted lat/lon mean, changes the values and breaks the agreement with CPC.

The reconstruction-minus-CPC residual is not white rounding noise: it drifts slowly from about -0.01 degC in the 1950s to about +0.02 degC in the 2010s. That drift is real and expected, and an answer that notices it is not wrong; it stays far inside the 2 decimal places CPC publishes and does not affect any graded number.
